# Consolidated Research Memorandum: Implementable Cognitive Mechanisms Across *How the Mind Works* and *Learnability and Cognition*

## Scope, Extraction Status, and Citation Discipline

This consolidation integrates eight second-reading memoranda covering Steven Pinker's *How the Mind Works*, file pages 1 through 455, and *Learnability and Cognition*, file pages 1 through 509. The substantive argument of *How the Mind Works* runs through file page 326, with endnotes at file pages 327 through 356 and apparatus thereafter; the substantive argument of *Learnability and Cognition* runs through file page 460, with notes and apparatus thereafter. Two extraction gaps matter for engineering: the visual figures in the vision chapter of *How the Mind Works*, including the semantic network diagram at file page 57, the neural-network figures at file pages 65 through 69, the Adelson zigzag drawings at file pages 142 through 143, the stereograms at file pages 130 through 137, the geon illustrations at file page 159, the shape stimuli at file pages 164 through 166, the imagery diagrams at file pages 170 through 172, and the infant displays at file pages 185 through 187, are described in prose but not visually recoverable; and the tree diagrams in *Learnability and Cognition* at file pages 95, 116, 228 through 232, 239 through 240, 250 through 251, 262 through 263, 268 through 309, and 447 through 448 are rendered as text fragments, so their logic is reportable from surrounding prose but their exact graphical layout is not verifiable. The musical notation at file pages 332 through 334 of *How the Mind Works* is likewise unrecoverable. All claims below rest on the memoranda as supplied; none has been silently repaired or relocated. Where a memorandum flags uncertainty, that uncertainty is preserved.

## The Representational Core: Structured Records with Explicit Roles

Pinker's central engineering claim in *How the Mind Works* is that intelligence is computation over symbols carrying both representational and causal roles, with rationality consisting in the machinery being arranged so that true inputs yield true outputs (file pages 66 through 67). The production system at file pages 45 through 49 makes this concrete: long-term memory holds typed propositions such as "Abel parent-of Me," short-term memory is a scratchpad, a goal area holds questions, and demons are condition-action reflexes that pattern-match, copy, erase, or print marks. One demon decomposes an uncle-of goal into subgoals for parents, siblings, and gender checks, then writes "Z uncle-of Y" to long-term store (file pages 45 through 49). The elementary operations are pattern match, guarded copy, erase, and write. Pinker hides variable binding as "minding its Ps and Qs" (file page 46), leaving role binding unsolved at this level.

*Learnability and Cognition* supplies the representational format that the production system lacks. Verb meanings are hybrid structures: a scaffolding of universal, grammatically relevant meaning elements plus slots for idiosyncratic conceptual information (file page 218). The scaffolding vocabulary includes conceptual constituents such as event, state, thing, path, place, property, and manner; predicates act, go, be, and have defined by features for dynamism and control; place-functions and path-functions; features of subordinating relations including cause-focus versus effect-focus, success versus failure, occurrence versus nonoccurrence, purposive, and deontic; object properties including animacy, humanness, dimensionality, count versus mass, rigidity, substance versus aggregate, and liquid versus semisolid; temporal objects including a time-line with points and regions; and mechanisms including open arguments, coindexing, semantic field annotation, and quoted constants (file page 265). Quoted constants are opaque to grammatical rules but point to rich conceptual content: a rule can be sensitive to whether a verb specifies that a location argument has some property, but cannot interpret the difference between butter and jam (file page 237).

Role binding is handled by coindexing. An argument can have thematic roles specified in several places in a semantic structure, but only one place serves as a trigger for a linking rule, symbolized by square brackets, with other positions annotated by an index (file page 251). The verb run, for example, has its agent coindexed with the theme of the resulting motion (file page 252). Linking rules map open arguments onto grammatical functions based on position in the tree: a theme maps to a direct internal argument, a goal to an indirect internal argument, a location to an indirect internal argument (file page 230); actors and agents map to external arguments, patients to direct internal arguments (file page 248). The biuniqueness constraint requires every open argument to link to exactly one function and no function to receive more than one argument (file page 108). Lexical rules transform one semantic structure into another: dativization converts "cause X to go to Y" into "cause Y to have X," causativization converts "Y changes" into "cause Y to change," locativization converts "cause X to go into or onto Y" into "cause Y to change state by means of putting X into or onto it," and passivization converts "X acts on Y" into "Y is in the circumstance of X acting on it" (file pages 96 through 97). The elementary operations underlying lexical rules include adding or deleting a cause argument, making a patient a theme, embedding an act as means, adding or deleting path, purpose, benefactive, or instrument arguments, assigning patient roles, and suppressing nonspecific arguments (file page 267). Pinker explicitly states that decomposing lexical rules into sets of these operations is beyond his scope, and that listing input and output structures is an expedient shortcut (file page 267). This is a genuine gap.

My engineering proposal, distinct from Pinker's claims, is that each semantic structure be implemented as a bounded-depth tree of typed nodes with explicit slots, each linking rule as a mapping from slot to grammatical role, and each lexical rule as an ordered set of the elementary operations applied to a tree, with unoperated parts carried over untouched, following the principle Pinker states at file page 266 but does not algorithmize. Composition happens through tree fusion: the open arguments of a verb's semantic structure are matched with the semantic structures of the phrases that fill them, and inconsistency produces semantic anomaly (file page 232). The example is that "the sand splashed" is anomalous because splash specifies that its argument be liquid (file page 236). I propose that fusion be implemented as tree unification with optional slots, but Pinker states at file page 270 that there is currently no format for the input structure of a rule and no matching function by which a semantic structure would be deemed to match a rule. This is an explicit acknowledgment of an unsolved problem.

Pinker's critique of associationism in *How the Mind Works* reinforces this representational constraint. Simply turning on units for "baby," "ate," and "slug" is insufficient because it does not specify who did what to whom; dedicating a node to each full combination explodes combinatorially, and concept-role pairs fail because no set of weights can distinguish "Baby same-as baby," "Baby different-from slug," "Slug different-from baby," and "Slug same-as slug" (file pages 74 through 75). His proposed solution, drawn from Geoffrey Hinton, is a separate layer of proposition units acting as arbitrary labels binding concepts into roles (file page 75), which closely mimics language-like mentalese and requires a distinction between concepts and roles plus machinery to bind each concept to its role properly (file page 75). Quantification and variable binding are named as necessary and left unsolved: logicians use variables and quantifiers to distinguish "every forty-five seconds someone is injured" from "there is someone who is injured every forty-five seconds," and "so far, we have no hint as to how this can be done in an associative network" (file page 76). Recursion is handled by a recursive transition network, with each simple structure stored once and a processor shuttling attention while storing the itinerary in short-term memory (file page 76), implementable as a stack of pointers with a state machine. My proposal is that the proposition layer be implemented as structured records with explicit slots rather than superimposed patterns, because superimposition produces the cross-talk and catastrophic forgetting Pinker documents at file pages 76 through 77.

## Perception, Grounding, and the Gap to Concepts

Pinker's account of vision in *How the Mind Works* specifies what a perception module must produce: not a picture, but a structured record in mentalese available to the rest of the mind through a shared blackboard (file page 127). The mechanism is constraint satisfaction. In stereo vision, the correspondence problem has combinatorially many possible matchings; Marr and Tomaso Poggio's network has input units for retinal points feeding an array of units for pairings, with units turning on only for matching input from both eyes, competing matches inhibiting one another, and neighboring points at nearby depths exciting one another, reverberating until stabilization (file pages 138 through 139). This is implementable as iterative relaxation over a lattice of candidate assignments. My proposal is that the same skeleton serve as a general-purpose inference engine: candidate hypotheses with confidence values, connected by excitatory and inhibitory links encoding domain assumptions, iterated to convergence or a resource limit. The source does not supply the scheduling policy, stopping criterion, or mechanism for combining solutions from different constraint networks.

Pinker notes the model is incomplete: people in artificial worlds violating uniqueness and smoothness do not perform as badly as predicted (file page 139), because the brain uses additional cues such as fine contour features and monocularly visible features at occlusion boundaries (file pages 139 through 140). The Adelson and Pentland workshop parable at file pages 147 through 151 is the key coordination proposal: a shape specialist, a lighting specialist, and a reflectance specialist each propose an interpretation, and a supervisor assigns costs, with simple and common operations cheap and complex and unusual ones expensive, and the cheapest overall interpretation winning (file pages 148 through 149). Their program passes a rigid three-dimensional model through an assembly line and settles on the interpretation people see (file pages 149 through 150). Pinker notes that exchanging guesses in a constraint network rather than an assembly line might produce the depth flips of the Necker cube (file page 150). My proposal is that the cost function be computed over structured records rather than scalar scores alone, because specialists must agree on shared bindings such as which surface belongs to which object and which edge is a paint boundary versus a shadow boundary. The source does not specify how such agreement is represented or enforced.

The output of vision is a two-and-a-half-dimensional sketch: a mosaic of cells each dedicated to a line of sight, holding depth, slant, tilt, color, and surface ownership for patches, or boundary type, orientation, and ownership for edges (file pages 153 through 154). This is viewer-centered, surface-based, and transient, not an object-centered categorical representation. Marr's question "Is a nose an object? Is a head one?" at file page 153 shows the definition of an object is problematic at this level. The gap between this sketch and a grounded concept symbol like "chair" is explicitly left open. The inverse optics problem at file pages 28 through 29 shows the retinal array is underdetermined, with the brain supplying assumptions such as smooth and uniform lighting; a three-step algorithm for surface lightness is given at file page 29, but the step from recovered surfaces to discrete symbols is deferred to Chapter 4, outside the first section.

Reference frames are directly relevant to role binding. The sketch is useless in retinal coordinates, which shift with eye movements (file page 154); the solution is a movable frame like a cursor, with the simplest being head-centered, maintained by copying the eye-movement command to a frame-shifting mechanism (file page 155), and other frames compensating for head and body movement or aligning with object axes (file pages 155 through 157). My proposal is that every spatial representation carry an explicit frame-of-reference tag as a first-class field, with a transformation module able to re-express spatial relations in any available frame. The source describes frames and empirical signatures but not the transformation algebra.

Pinker's two theories of symbol meaning in *How the Mind Works* are causal and inferential-role. The causal theory says a symbol is connected to its referent through sense organs: a mother's face reflects light, triggering a cascade that inscribes the symbol (file page 81). The inferential-role theory says a symbol means what it does because of the pattern of inferences it participates in. Pinker argues both are needed, kept in sync by natural selection designing perception and inference to work accurately (file page 81). For implementation, every primitive symbol must have a causal anchor, a sensorimotor pathway that can create and verify it, and an inferential role, a set of demons that read and write it. The mechanism converting a percept into a mentalese symbol is not given.

*Learnability and Cognition* states that conceptual structures are formed by perception of the situations in which verbs are used, providing constraints outside the linguistic system (file page 227), but does not describe the perceptual process. The Grammatically Relevant Subsystem hypothesis holds that verb meanings are organized around a set of semantic elements much smaller than the cognitively available distinctions (file page 215), and these elements must be meaningful, with translations into conceptual terms that define the range of situations in which a verb could truthfully be used (file page 218). The example is that the notion of an effect allows us to decide that rubbing a knife against a steel pipe with no change in the latter is not cutting (file page 218). Pinker lists what Talmy claims languages encode: main event as state or motion, path, direction, location, causation, manner, properties of theme or actor, temporal distribution, purpose, coreferentiality, and truth value (file page 223), and what they rarely encode: mood, attitude, hedging, rate of motion, symmetry, color, person, gender, tense, and more (file page 223). This constrains the vocabulary a perceptual front end would need to produce, but does not tell us how to compute those elements from sensor readings. My proposal is that the machine need a perceptual front end producing candidate event descriptions in the same vocabulary as the semantic scaffolding: things with properties, moving along paths, acting on other things, causing effects. The mapping from raw data to those descriptions is entirely unsolved in both texts.

Grounding must go beyond labels. Pinker's causal theory requires sensorimotor pathways, and *Learnability and Cognition* requires that geometric and material properties of locative verbs be attached to the theme argument in the motion structure rather than the patient in the action structure, because properties of an object loaded into a container are interdependent with the container's shape and the liquidity of sprayed stuff is related to the shape it assumes while moving (file pages 472 through 473). This is a claim about where causal and informational grounding must be represented: object properties must bind to the moving participant, or cross-situational generalization will fail. My proposal is that grounding be established through observations and interventions, with each perceptual record carrying a pointer to the sensory source and time of registration, so the system can distinguish remembered from currently perceived content, a distinction the index of *How the Mind Works* associates with reality monitoring at file page 379 but does not mechanismize.

## Learning, Generalization, and Revision

Pinker's position in *How the Mind Works* is that learning is performed by innate machinery, with different modules learning according to different logics (file page 33), and he rejects the framing of innateness versus learning as unhelpful. The concrete mechanisms described are error correction in pattern associators (file pages 68 through 69), backpropagation for hidden layers (file page 69), and the Baldwin effect, in which learning guides evolution by making partially correct innate structures viable (file pages 78 through 79). None is a complete account of concept acquisition or revision. The discussion of crisp versus fuzzy categories at file pages 77 through 80 is directly relevant: people form fuzzy stereotypes by soaking up correlations but also construct rule systems defining categories sharply and supporting deduction (file pages 79 through 80). My proposal is that the architecture need both a similarity-based generalizer for prototype formation and an explanation-based generalizer using rules to project properties, sharing a common structured-record format so a similarity match can propose a category assignment that a rule system can elaborate or override. The source names both but does not specify the arbitration process.

*Learnability and Cognition* supplies the learning problem in detail. Baker's paradox is that infinitely many hypotheses fit a finite sample, and a hypothesis generating a superset of the target language cannot be falsified by positive evidence alone (file page 27). Parents do not differentially approve or disapprove grammatical versus ungrammatical utterances (file page 28), and subtle feedback such as repetitions is noisy, not uniformly contingent on ungrammaticality, and not demonstrably used by children (file pages 32 through 37); a child saying "Nobody don't like me" resisted eight rounds of overt correction (file page 35). This rules out learning by trial and error with external correction. Children produce passives, double-object datives, causatives, and locatives with invented verbs never heard in those forms (file pages 42 through 51), with elicitation rates for productive passives at nineteen to eighty-one percent of opportunities, double-object datives at forty to fifty-three percent, lexical causatives at fifty-five to sixty-six percent, and container-object locatives at seventy-eight to one hundred percent (file page 54). A control condition with a pseudoargument structure produced it only four percent of the time, against fifty percent for the double-object form (file page 54), showing children are not simply complying with demand.

Pinker's answer is that the learner is constrained by the format of its representations and the operations acting on them. The constraints fall out of what rules do to semantic structures (file pages 81 through 135). The learning sequence at file page 82 is: record argument structures, note recurring patterns, create productive rules, note verbs failing to occur in one form, search for a property distinguishing the two groups, constrain the rule, and replace the constraint if falsified. Two processes operate in parallel for verb meanings: Event-Category Labeling, mapping a sound onto a preexisting conceptual structure for a recurring event type (file page 320), and Semantic Structure Hypothesis Testing, maintaining a maximal candidate semantic structure and permanently erasing any component contradicted by the current situation (file page 322). The example is fill: the child could encode agent-patient relation, manner of causing liquid to move, that the moving thing is liquid, manner of movement, container shape, end state, and agent's goal; over instances, contradicted structures are erased and an accurate representation survives (file page 322). My proposal is that this be implemented as candidate nodes attached to each verb record, with deletion triggered whenever perceptual input fails to instantiate a candidate node. Pinker specifies the logic but not the data structures or matching algorithm.

Three constraints prune the hypothesis space: semantic biases so children assemble cohesive scenarios rather than random combinations, discourse contexts especially contrastive ones, and the Principle of Contrast that virtually no two words have the same meaning (file page 323). For a machine, this means pruning by a similarity metric over semantic structures, with a new verb entry differing from every existing entry in at least one grammatically relevant respect. I supply the implementation as a tree comparison operation; Pinker states the principle but not the algorithm.

Syntactic cueing provides direct evidence about argument structure from overt phrases in argument positions (file page 324), and universal linking rules can be applied backward: a semantically indeterminate noun phrase in object position suggests an open patient slot (file page 325). A two-step procedure uses linking rules in reverse to acquire conflation classes, then uses those classes to drive learning of semantic structures (file page 326). The example is that a child with the English conflation class for GO-THING-PATH-MANNER verbs hearing "The ball glipped into the room" could guess that the current manner of motion is encoded into glip (file page 326). My proposal is a library of conflation class templates with open slots for idiosyncratic information, instantiated when a new verb is encountered in a known argument structure. Pinker describes the logic but not the template representation or matching function.

The circularity problem is that an incorrect semantic structure could derive a conflation class used to hypothesize incorrect meanings for syntactically similar verbs (file page 327). Hypothesis testing must be the final arbiter, an inspector pruning any branch not standing up to confrontation with the conceptual world; syntax-guided learning only guides the formation of likely hypotheses (file page 327). Landau and Gleitman's proposal that syntactic formats narrow meaning components cannot play a foundational role, because components predictable from argument structure are those shared by many verbs in that structure, not the idiosyncratic core (file page 330). The example is that "The ball floated into the cave" must not be evidence that float has to do with moving into, since a ball can float without moving; the into phrase implies movement into, predictable from into itself (file page 330). In the limit, examining more argument structures leaves exactly the idiosyncratic meaning associated with a sound in the brute-force listing (file page 331), as in the riddle whose answer is sewing (file page 331). This is cognitive problem solving, not direct backward application of linguistic contingencies. For a machine, syntactic cueing can constrain the hypothesis space but cannot replace perceptual grounding for the idiosyncratic core.

Broad conflation classes are derived by applying linking rules backward from grammatical functions, then completing the skeleton by extracting information shared by all verbs in the class (file pages 333 through 334). For the prepositional dative, this gives an ACT structure with agent and patient slots and a to path, integrated into a single-rooted connected graph (file page 333); examining lexical entries adds that the GO structure is embedded via an effect link and a coreference link joins the patient of the ACT and the theme of the GO (file page 334). My proposal is tree intersection: compute the greatest common subtree shared by all verb entries in a class and store it as the thematic core. Pinker describes the logic but not the algorithm. He notes that examining arguments in a particular order and intertwining skeleton building with lexical abstraction has computational advantages, and that top-down linking and bottom-up lexical information may be so intertwined that separate algorithms are a convenient fiction, better viewed as constraints simultaneously satisfied (file page 335). This suggests a constraint satisfaction architecture rather than a sequential pipeline.

Narrow conflation classes are learned by replacing each idiosyncratic piece of information in a verb's semantic structure with a parameter, so the class embraces all verbs with identical structure up to idiosyncratic information (file page 343). The effect is knowledge that an item sharing grammatically relevant information but differing in manner or object property is a possible verb (file page 343). Narrow-range rules contain nodes dominated by the same nodes as the open arguments remapped by the broad-range rule, or coindexed with such arguments, with deeper substructures parameterized by a single symbol (file page 345). The strong hypothesis of Color-Blind Conservatism holds that grammar is basically conservative but cannot see most cognitive distinctions (file page 347), following from conservatism, grammatically relevant semantic subvocabulary, and independence of morphology from lexical listing (file page 347). The matching function may be more flexible than exact match up to constants substituted for variables; a metric allowing one difference would not damage the account, since narrow classes scatter through multidimensional semantic space (file page 349). Some structures are more important in drawing boundaries: major aspectual differences, event type differences, major semantic fields, and object properties in different positions block productivity, while others may not be fatal (file page 350). My proposal is a weighted matching function with hard and soft constraints; Pinker describes the qualitative distinction but not the weighting scheme.

The autonomy of lexical semantics is decisive for grounding. Verb meanings are not scripts, frames, stereotypes, or feature clusters computed by general similarity, but constraints on which aspects of an event the verb is choosy about (file pages 146 through 148). The semantics of kiss do not require prior motion resulting in contact, and the semantics of break do not require motion followed by contact (file page 147). What matters is what the representation imposes conditions on, not what typically happens. A machine clustering events by statistical similarity will group kiss with hug and break with shatter in ways that do not predict syntactic behavior. The machine needs a representation marking which aspects are constrained and which are open. My proposal is that each semantic record carry explicit constraint fields alongside open fields, and that the learning operation assigning a verb to a conflation class inspect only the constraint fields. Pinker describes the distinction but gives no algorithm for extracting constraint fields from perceptual experience.

Narrow classes solve the problem that coarse criteria are necessary but not sufficient (file pages 136 through 142). "Throw Mary the ball" is grammatical but "carry Mary the ball" is not; "ask Mary a question" is grammatical but "shout Mary a question" is not (file page 137). Broad classes provide necessary conditions, narrow classes sufficient conditions (file page 142). For transitive action verbs, the conative alternation applies to motion followed by contact such as hit and cut but not touching or breaking; part-possessor ascension applies to contact but not breaking; contact locative applies to motion followed by contact but not effect; middle applies to effect; anticausative applies to effect but nothing else (file pages 143 through 145). The lexicon cannot be a flat list but a structured inventory of subclasses determined by semantic elements present in constraint fields (file page 146 lists motion, contact, effect). My proposal is that each verb store a set of semantic elements from a small vocabulary, and each lexical rule specify which element combinations it licenses, firing only on match.

Negative exceptions persist even with narrow classes (file pages 149 through 163). Verbs that should alternate by coarse criteria do not (file page 137), and semantic compatibility alone cannot rule them out; dialect differences show shout him the answer and carry him the box grammatical in some dialects (file page 138). Pinker's response is that language guards verbs' grammatically relevant semantic structures vigilantly (file page 140), with new meanings assigned only in precise circumstances defined by narrow classes (file page 141). Verbs of instantaneous imparting of force causing ballistic motion can be reconstrued as causing possession, but verbs of continuous exertion causing accompanied motion cannot, even though both are cognitively compatible with change of possession (file page 141). The distinction is linguistic, not cognitive. The hardest part for a machine is learning which narrow classes exist and their partly arbitrary boundaries (file page 148). The conditions are motivated but not deducible a priori (file page 148), and historical processes favor verbs exemplifying the semantic structure created by the rule (file page 148), a claim about language change, not a learning algorithm. My proposal is a hypothesis space of candidate narrow classes defined by combinations of semantic elements, revised when verbs violate current boundaries. The list of possible criteria must be finite and not too large, or the child might never find the relevant one, and Pinker concedes it is difficult to come up with an explicit list (file page 91).

The notes in *Learnability and Cognition* add qualifications. Note 4 at file page 465 warns that motivated categories may be opaque to speakers, with well-formedness judgments more discriminating than theorist motivations, and motivations unpredictable in advance, so motivated classes must be learned as lists at least part of the time. This blocks any design where a similarity metric automatically generates the right classes. My proposal is that class membership be stored as explicit listed data alongside derived similarity structure, with listed data taking precedence on conflict; the precedence rule is mine. Note 5 at file page 465 gives verbs like butter, reward, credit, supply incorporating a theme paraphrasable as causing a substance to go to a target, with optional with-objects adding nonredundant information; "He buttered the bread with butter" and "He rewarded her with a reward" are degraded because the with-object repeats the incorporated nominal. An implementable representation stores a cause relation, motion or transfer relation, and theme node fixed by the verb root, plus a constraint that any with-argument contribute a node not already present; the operation is a redundancy check over shared subtrees. The paraphrase and constraint are Pinker's; the tree and check are mine. Note 8 at file pages 465 through 466 handles lexical ambiguity: food-preparation verbs like pour, boil, fry appear counterexamples to a creation requirement in the double-object, but food terms are ambiguous between raw material and consumable product, and the verbs entail creation before giving, supported by "Can you pour me a cup of coffee" being better than "Can you pour me that coffee" and "She cooked me some pork" better than "She cooked me a pig." The semantic analyzer must represent a single object with multiple type nodes, and the double-object rule must match the consumable-product node; the ambiguity analysis is Pinker's, the multi-type representation mine. Note 12 at file page 466 flags sprinkle as borderline between downward applied force and force causing motion in a spatial distribution, with shake confined to one class, and Pinker declines to explore a third cause involving phonological similarity to spatter and splash; this is genuinely unresolved. Note 14 at file pages 466 through 467 gives a naturalistic example of cereal ribboning into the custard as a distinct area versus being mixed throughout, showing content-versus-container choice tracks geometry of distribution. Note 20 at file pages 467 through 468 lists positive exceptions learned itemwise: rattle only by shaking, leak of secrets but not water, bleed of pipes but not clothing, smoke of cigarettes and ham but not firewood or butter, transitive shine restricted to polish or direct a beam. Note 21 at file page 468 adds that anticausativization applies only to causative verbs that could have been formed by causativization to begin with, with no lexical specification of direction, manner, or instrument motion. The lexicon must carry per-item idiosyncratic restrictions overriding general rules, and rule applicability must
